messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Seventeen years ago, Ajay had been driving home from a late clinic shift when the brake line gave way and his car skidded across the slick asphalt of the interstate. The impact was jarring—his head hit the steering wheel, his spine bent in a way he never imagined, and he felt the world shatter into fragments. The ambulance’s sirens later rang in the silence of his apartment, a reminder that the accident had left him physically scarred and mentally rattled. The next days, he woke up sweating and his heart pounding at the very sound of the wind’s whistling through the apartment blinds, and he began to notice a new kind of terror whenever the house was noisy: the sudden clatter of a falling object, a neighbor’s loud television, even the hum of his own heart seemed to echo with a looming threat. The intrusive images that returned unbidden, the dream residue that left him half‑awake and jittery, and the constant startle to loud noises made Ajay hypervigilant. He was afraid that the next day’s lecture on therapeutic exercise would turn into another disaster. These triggers spurred him to scan his surroundings for weapons, to think of worst‑case scenarios, and to obsessively clean and organize his office. Every time his mind spiraled toward a memory of the crash, he felt a surge of physical vulnerability, a conviction that his body was permanently damaged and unreliable, and a fear that anyone could harm him at any moment. The belief that his own body could no longer be trusted pushed him to repeat the cleaning rituals, a strategy that he believed would bring a fragile sense of control. The more he rehearsed the worst, the more he felt that he was truly prepared, but the rehearsals also kept the intrusive thoughts alive. The presence of potential weapons—any sharp or dangerous object in his environment—became a source of ongoing threat. This awareness fed back into his negative appraisals, reinforcing the idea that he could never trust his own body and that harm was inevitable. The constant threat perception in turn sharpened his triggers: the sound of a doorbell would spark a flash of the collision, and the sight of a misplaced box would ignite a flashback, perpetuating the cycle of fear. As the cleaning compulsions intensified, Ajay found that the very act of arranging objects often revealed hidden dangers he had previously ignored, further heightening his threat perception. Each new layer of threat reinforced his belief that his body was a fragile machine, vulnerable to any unexpected assault, and that the only way to survive was to maintain a state of hyper‑alertness. In the weeks that followed, the relentless cycle of triggers, threat, negative appraisals, and maladaptive strategies began to bleed into his professional life. The physical therapist he was, who once guided patients with patience and calm, now struggled to focus on patient education because his mind kept drifting to the next possible hazard. He became chronically tired, his concentration slipping, and he started missing appointments, citing “a quick check” to ensure no sharp objects remained in the treatment room. His wife, Lila, noticed his unease; she asked him about the constant cleaning, but he would deflect, saying that it was just a habit to keep the office safe. The strain on their relationship grew, and the sense of isolation that followed the accident left Ajay feeling alone in a world that seemed increasingly hostile. Despite the practical adjustments he made, Ajay could not shake the feeling that something terrible was waiting just around the corner. He began to dread the very sound of traffic, fearing that the next crash could happen to him or his family. The dream residue that left him disoriented at dawn made him question whether his days could ever return to normal. It was the culmination of this chronic anxiety, the loss of concentration, and the constant mental rehearsal of disaster that pushed him to finally seek help. He was certain that his body was still unsafe, that the world around him was filled with unseen threats, and that his compulsions were merely a thin veil of control over a reality that had taken away much of his sense of safety. In the clinic, he hopes to learn a way to calm his mind and restore trust in his own body, so that he can return to his patients without the looming sense that any noise or object might be the harbinger of another catastrophic event.
